title: Enhancing medical anomaly detection via text-adapted few-shot learning with visual-language models

text: Medical image anomaly detection (AD) is crucial for early disease diagnosis, yet it faces challenges such as data heterogeneity and scarcity of annotated samples. This paper introduces a text-adapted few-shot training framework using CLIP, which extends the text encoder to incorporate ﬁne-grained descriptions and introduces a text feature adapter for better alignment with image representations. A text-image feature alignment module and a contrastive learning mechanism are presented to enhance cross-modal integration and the distinction between normal and abnormal samples. Experimental evaluations on six medical imaging datasets demonstrate that our method signiﬁcantly outperforms stateof-the-art techniques in both classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks, achieving an average improvement of 1.13% in AUC. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/clownddd/TAFT. Keywords: Few-shot learning, Medical image anomaly detection, Text feature adapter, Text-image feature alignment, Contrastive learning 1
title: Enhancing medical anomaly detection via text-adapted few-shot learning with visual-language models

text: Anomaly detection (AD) in medical imaging aims to identify patterns that deviate from normal anatomical structures or physiological appearances. It plays a crucial role in early disease diagnosis and clinical decision support, providing valuable insights for disease management. AD is intrinsically a problem of image classiﬁcation and segmentation, which are fundamental tasks in the ﬁeld of computer vision. Therefore, with the development of deep learning technology, research on anomaly detection methods has also achieved signiﬁcant progress [1–3]. However, this ﬁeld still faces dual challenges. From the data perspective, due to the diversity of anomalies in medical images, the heterogeneity of data generated by multimodal imaging devices (such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound), and the signiﬁcant diﬀerences between diﬀerent anatomical regions, traditional unimodal modeling methods ﬁnd it diﬃcult to achieve cross-domain generalization. From the supervision perspective, medical image annotation requires the involvement of professional physicians, and the annotation cost is high, resulting in a severe scarcity of training data. These two major limitations make normalsample-based training methods diﬃcult to adapt to the complex cross-modal detection demands in real clinical environments. Due to these two defects, addressing the constraints of vision representation in medical image anomaly detection under few-shot learning conditions has attracted increasing attention. Multimodal AD incorporates class-level text but lacks ﬁne-grained alignment. Our method introduces ﬁne-grained text, a text adapter, and an alignment module to enhance cross-modal feature fusion and anomaly detection. In existing studies, few-shot AD methods aim to improve the generalization performance of models under data-scarce conditions, although each new AD task still requires lightweight re-training [4–6] or distributional adaptation [7]. Recent progress in large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) has signiﬁcantly advanced few-shot medical image analysis. A notable example is CLIP [8], which achieves cross-modal alignment by leveraging manually designed text prompts. Innovative works have 2 adapted CLIP for anomaly detection. Peng et al. [9] designed an image-to-text feature adapter. Huang et al. [10] proposed a hierarchical adaptation framework. Jongheo et al. [11] optimized textual prompts through engineering strategies. Despite their promising results, these methods fundamentally overlook the inherent complementarity between visual and text representations, particularly for ﬁne-grained pathological discrimination. These methods adopt a naive implementation of CLIP’s text encoder, where binary class descriptors (”normal/abnormal”) generate textual embeddings to complement visual features. They report that such text-driven augmentation yields limited performance gains. However, our analysis reveals that the texture representation patterns learned by CLIP from natural image corpora are ill-suited for capturing ﬁne-grained features speciﬁc to medical image abnormal detection. Furthermore, the CLIP text encoder does not

text: CLIP’s text encoder, where binary class descriptors (”normal/abnormal”) generate textual embeddings to complement visual features. They report that such text-driven augmentation yields limited performance gains. However, our analysis reveals that the texture representation patterns learned by CLIP from natural image corpora are ill-suited for capturing ﬁne-grained features speciﬁc to medical image abnormal detection. Furthermore, the CLIP text encoder does not eﬀectively align with the semantic space necessary to address the challenges posed by abnormal detection. These observations indicate that existing methods have not yet fully exploited the potential of CLIP for medical image anomaly detection, and further in-depth investigation is required. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a text-adapted training framework for few-shot medical image anomaly detection with CLIP, as shown in Figure 1. Through minimal modiﬁcations, we leverage the cross-modal collaborative potential to enhance model performance. First, to fully exploit the representation capabilities of CLIP’s text encoder, we extend the textual descriptions from class-level to region-level, thereby enhancing the granularity of the text descriptions. Additionally, we introduce an extra adapter to the text encoder, improving its adaptability to medical image semantics. Second, we design an image-text feature alignment module, enabling better alignment and fusion of multimodal features between text and image. Lastly, during the ﬁnal feature map generation stage, we incorporate a contrastive learning constraint to further increase the feature distance between normal and abnormal samples, thereby improving discriminative capability of the model. In the training phase, for each dataset, we randomly select a small number of labeled samples, typically 2, 4, 8, or 16 normal samples and the same number of abnormal samples as the few-shot training set. These few samples are used to ﬁnetune the lightweight modules, while keeping the CLIP backbone frozen. In the testing phase, the adapted image features are compared with the processed text features and the additional referenced image features. Anomaly scores are computed through feature similarity for both classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks. The main contributions are summarized below:: • We extend the CLIP text encoder with ﬁne-grained descriptions and introduce an adapter to the text encoder. This design bridges the semantic granularity gap between text and image features, enabling ﬁne-grained representation of medical anomalies under few-shot conditions. • We design a multi-level text-image alignment module to improve cross-modal semantic consistency, and incorporate a supervised contrastive learning strategy to explicitly enhance the model’s capability to distinguish between normal and abnormal samples. 3 • We conducted extensive experiments on six benchmark medical datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks. Ablation studies further validate the contribution of each component.

text: Anomaly detection aims to identify patterns that deviate from the normal distribution. The main challenge lies in building robust normal feature representations and quantifying the deviation between normal and abnormal samples. Recent studies have further explored medical image segmentation by enhancing feature representation and contextual modeling. For example, Cfseg-Net [12] emphasizes context feature extraction, while D2U-Net [13] adopts a dual-path hybrid U-Net architecture to capture complementary representations for precise segmentation. In addition, many methods focus on unsupervised techniques that rely solely on normal samples [14–24],. For instance, PatchCore [19] constructs a memory bank of normal samples and detects anomalies based on their proximity to test samples. Similarly, CﬂowAD [17] uses normalizing ﬂows to map normal samples to a Gaussian distribution. However, using only normal samples can lead to ambiguous decision boundaries and limited discriminative ability [25]. Incorporating a few abnormal samples can enhance performance by providing clearer decision boundaries. In medical image anomaly detection, challenges like modality diversity and complex lesion shapes must be addressed. Current methods often treat anomaly detection as a one-class problem, using only normal images for training [10]. For example, Jiang et al. proposed the Multi-scale Cross-restoration method [26], combining global and local features via a dual-branch autoencoder. Cai et al. introduced the Dualdistribution Discrepancy method [27], utilizing both normal and unlabeled images through self-supervised learning. Zhang et al. developed the Conﬁdence-Aware method [3], incorporating a conﬁdence module to reduce false positives. These approaches struggle with insuﬃcient model training. We address the limitations by incorporating contrastive learning, leveraging both normal and abnormal samples to improve model discrimination.

text: In scenarios with limited labeled data, existing studies primarily focus on few-shot learning and cross-domain transfer learning. For instance, Few-shot GAN [28] generates pseudo-anomalous samples by interpolating in the latent space to augment the training set. DRA [4] disentangles and reconstructs anomalies for generalizable detection, including unseen anomaly cases. WinCLIP [11] explores retrieval-based models in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection, using language modality to assist the detection process. Building on WinCLIP, April-GAN [29] maps visual features from CLIP into the linear space of text features, where the text features are located, supervised by 4 pixel-level annotated data. In addition, methods often fail to establish eﬀective semantic correlations across modalities, which are essential for medical anomaly detection. Our proposed cross-modal alignment mechanism directly addresses this challenge.

section: 2.3 Few-shot Medical Image Anomaly Detection with
text: Vision-Language Model Recently, large-scale vision-language models, such as CLIP [8], have demonstrated signiﬁcant advantages in cross-modal learning for medical image anomaly detection. By aligning 400 million image-text pairs from natural domains, these models enable zero-shot and few-shot learning. Several studies have explored applying CLIP to medical anomaly detection. For example, CLIP-Adapter [9] introduces an image feature adapter to map medical image features into the shared text feature space. MVFA [10] proposes a multi-level feature adaptation framework for optimizing representations at diﬀerent levels, while WinCLIP [30] uses prompt engineering to guide CLIP’s text features for medical applications. These methods directly use the text encoder module without fully leveraging the potential CLIP. The text encoder is primarily optimized for class-level semantics, not ﬁne-grained features, and it emphasizes global rather than local details. This paper addresses these limitations by utilizing several tricks to better exploit the text encoder’s capabilities and unlock the full potential of CLIP. However, these methods often neglect the potential improvements on CLIP’s text encoder. CLIP’s text encoder is primarily designed for object-level semantics, not anomalyspeciﬁc semantics, and it focuses on global features. Given that medical anomalies often manifest in localized details, existing CLIP-based methods may struggle to accurately localize and identify such anomalies.

text: We enhance CLIP for few-shot medical anomaly detection by introducing ﬁne-grained text descriptions and a text adapter. The text features, after being processed by the adapter, are aligned and fused with the image features. The fused representation is then used for joint contrastive learning across diﬀerent fusion class, and ﬁnally aligned with the ground-truth labels. The structure of our proposed method is illustrated in Figure 2.

text: We formalize the task of anomaly detection (AD) in medical imaging as follows. Let D = {(xi, ci, pi)}n i=1 denote a medical image dataset containing n samples, where each sample consists of an image xi, an class-level label ci ∈{0, 1}, and a region-level label pi ∈{0, 1}h×w. Speciﬁcally, xi is the input medical image, ci = 0 denotes a normal image and ci = 1 indicates an anomalous image, while pi deﬁnes a binary segmentation mask over the image of spatial resolution h×w, with pi(j, k) = 1 indicating the region at position (j, k) is anomalous. Given a model F, the goal is to simultaneously predict 5 Fig. 2 During training, ﬁne-grained text descriptions and a text adapter enhance CLIP’s text encoder, enabling ﬁne-grained alignment with visual features via multi-level fusion. A joint contrastive loss further improves the separation between normal and abnormal patterns. At test time, anomaly scores are computed through both a zero-shot path and a few-shot path, which are ensembled for ﬁnal prediction. the class-level anomaly classiﬁcation label c and the region-level anomaly segmentation map p for a test image x, which can be shown as F(x) = {c, p}. The core challenge of this task lies in accurately identifying and localizing anomalous regions with only a limited number of annotated training samples, typically with n ∈{2, 4, 8, 16}, which reﬂects the few-shot learning setting commonly encountered in real-world medical scenarios. To enable anomaly detection on previously unseen imaging modalities and anatomical regions, we adopt a few-shot learning paradigm. Our training set comprises a limited collection of K annotated images drawn from the same modality and anatomical region as the test samples, where K is typically small (e.g., {2, 4, 8, 16} in this study). In the following, we sequentially present the novel techniques employed in this work.

text: In standard CLIP-based frameworks for medical anomaly detection, textual prompts are typically formulated at the image level, using simple class descriptors such as ”normal” or ”abnormal” to guide the feature extraction process. To enable ﬁne-grained alignment between visual and textual modalities, we extend CLIP’s original class-level textual descriptions to a region-level formulation, as shown in Figure 2. Speciﬁcally, we 6 Fig. 3 Expand the class-level textual data to the region-level using Compositional Prompt Ensemble. ﬁrst divide each input image into multiple patches according to the available regionlevel annotations. Each patch is labeled as either ”normal” or ”abnormal” based on the majority voting of the regional annotations within the patch. For each labeled patch, we generate a localized textual description that reﬂects both the position and appearance attributes of the corresponding region. This results in a rich set of regionlevel textual descriptions, each tightly coupled with a speciﬁc region of the image. For all region-level text descriptions, we concatenate them together and input them as a whole into the text encoder. This strategy eﬀectively bridges the granularity gap between global textual semantics and localized visual features, facilitating more accurate alignment and fusion in downstream classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks. As illustrated in Figure 2, we design a learnable text feature adapter A. section: 3.3 Alignment and Fusion of Image and Text
text: To bridge the semantic gap between visual features and textual descriptions, we introduce a multi-stage Alignment & Fusion module at each layer of the backbone. This module takes the output features from each Image Adapter (Fcls,4, Fseg,4) and aligns them with the text features generated by the Text Adapter. According to CLIP’s design philosophy, the highest-level visual features Fcls,4/Fseg,4 should share a semantic space with the textual features Ac(textf) and Ap(textf), respectively. To enforce such alignment, we introduce a supervised contrastive loss: Lalign = Lsup(Fcls,4/Fseg,4, Ac(Ftext)0/Ap(Ftext)0, Ac(Ftext)1/Ap(Ftext)1) (3) 8 Fig. 5 The alignment and fusion mechanisms of image-text features. where Lsup is the Supervised Contrastive Loss, while Ac(Ftext)0 and Ap(Ftext)0 denote textual features describing normal patterns, and Ac(Ftext)1, Ap(Ftext)1 correspond to abnormal ones. This alignment mechanism ensures that visual and textual features converge in a shared semantic space, particularly at the most abstract levels, facilitating more eﬀective joint reasoning for both classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks. For the fusion between text features and image features, we employ the tensor product (⊗) between visual and textual features to capture cross-modal interactions at each layer. This operation fuses class-level image features Fcls with Ac(Ftext), and region-level image features Fseg with Ap(Ftext), which fuses the visual and textual features at the corresponding levels separately.

section: 3.4 Joint Comparison of Image-Text Fusion Features
text: To further enhance the discriminability between normal and abnormal patterns across modalities, we design a Joint Comparison Loss module that supervises the ﬁnal fused features from both image and text pathways. After multi-level fusion and alignment, we obtain aggregated image features fc, fp and textual features Ac(textf), Ap(textf). They are fused via a tensor product to generate modality-aware prediction maps maskc and maskp, which correspond to class-level and pixel-level outputs, and are used as the ﬁnal result.To enforce a clear separation between matched and mismatched combinations of visual and textual semantics, we formulate a supervised contrastive loss as follows: Ljoint = Sup �mask(0,0) c/p , mask(1,1) c/p , mask(0,1) c/p , mask(1,0) c/p  (4) where: • mask(0,0) c/p denotes the fusion result of a normal image feature with a normal text description; • mask(1,1) c/p represents the fusion of abnormal image and abnormal text; 9 • mask(0,1) c/p and mask(1,0) c/p are cross-type combinations (normal-abnormal, or abnormal-normal). This loss encourages the model to bring matched (0, 0)/(1, 1) pairs closer in representation space while pushing apart mismatched (0, 1)/(1, 0) pairs, thereby amplifying the semantic distinction between normal and abnormal patterns at both global and local levels.Together with the alignment loss, this joint comparison mechanism improves the model’s ability to distinguish samples of diﬀerent categories when training data is insuﬃcient.

text: We adopt a multi-task loss function to jointly optimize the model on both pixellevel and class-level tasks.For the pixel-level segmentation, we use the Focal Loss to supervise the diﬀerence between the predicted segmentation mask maskp and the ground truth mask p. The loss is deﬁned as: Lfocal = FocalLoss(maskp, p) (5) where maskp denotes the predicted pixel-wise output, and p is the ground-truth pixellevel anomaly mask. For the class-levell classiﬁcation, we employ the Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) Loss to optimize the predicted classiﬁcation output maskc against the ground truth label c. This loss is deﬁned as: Lbce = BCE(maskc, c) (6) where maskc represents the predicted class-level result, and c is the corresponding binary classiﬁcation label (normal or abnormal). In addition to these task-speciﬁc losses,combined with the previously mentioned Alignment Loss and Joint Comparison Loss, our ﬁnal loss is deﬁned as follows: L = Lalign + Ljoint + Lfocal + Lbce (7) Through this joint optimization framework, our model eﬀectively improves both pixel-level anomaly localization and class-level anomaly classiﬁcation performance.

text: To enable eﬀective prediction of class-level anomaly classiﬁcation (AC) and pixel-level anomaly segmentation (AS), we design a dual-path testing architecture, consisting of a zero-shot branch and a few-shot branch. Each path produces anomaly scores from diﬀerent perspectives and is ﬁnally combined for ensemble prediction. Zero-Shot Branch. Given a test image xtest, it is processed through the Multilevel Visual Feature Adapter (MVFA) to generate a set of adapted visual features {Fcls,l, Fseg,l}4 l=1, where l denotes the adaptation level. These features are compared against a ﬁxed set of text features Ftext ∈R2×d, which encode normal and abnormal 10 textual prompts.The zero-shot anomaly classiﬁcation and segmentation scores, czero and Szero, are computed as follows: czero = 1 4 4 X l=1 max g∈G �softmax(Fcls,lF⊤ text)  , (8) Szero = 1 4 4 X l=1 BI �softmax(Fseg,lF⊤ text)  , (9) where G is the set of spatial grid locations, and BI(·) denotes bilinear interpolation to upsample the anomaly map to the original image resolution. Few-Shot Branch. In the few-shot branch, we leverage a memory bank G, constructed from multi-level features of a few annotated normal reference images. For a given test image, the nearest neighbor search computes the similarity between test features and stored normal patterns at each level. The anomaly classiﬁcation and segmentation scores from the few-shot branch are: cfew = 1 4 4 X l=1 max g∈G  min m∈G Dist(Fcls,l, F(m) cls,l)  , (10) Sfew = 1 4 4 X l=1 BI  min m∈G Dist(Fseg,l, F(m) seg,l)  , (11) where Dist(·, ·) = 1 −cos(·, ·) is the cosine distance, and F(m) denotes features of the m-th reference image in the memory bank. Final Prediction. The two branches are ensembled using weighting factors β1 and β2 (set to 0.5 by default) to produce the ﬁnal prediction scores: cpred = β1czero + β2cfew, Spred = β1Szero + β2Sfew. (12) Here, cpred determines the class-level anomaly label (Normal or Abnormal), and Spred provides a ﬁne-grained segmentation of the anomalous regions.

text: As shown in Table 1, our proposed method TAFT achieves competitive and often superior performance across multiple datasets in the few-shot anomaly detection setting (K=4). For datasets that also provide pixel-level labels we report both classiﬁcation accuracy(AC) and segmentation accuracy(AS), while for dataset that only provide class-level labels we report only classiﬁcation accuracy. Comparison with the full-normal-shot methods. In Table 1 we contrast our TAFT model with classical “normal-only’ methods that are trained on all available normal images. TAFT achieves the best results on every benchmark against the four full-normal-shot methods: CFlowAD, RD4AD, PatchCore and MKD. Comparison with the few-normal-shot methods. Compared with CLIP and WinCLIP—which rely on only a handful of normal images—our approach (TAFT) achieves markedly higher AUC on every dataset, conﬁrming that region-level prompts, text adaptation and a small set of abnormal examples give stronger generalisation than normal-only feature matching. Against MedCLIP we also lead on ﬁve of the six 12 benchmarks, and the sole exception is ChestXray, where MedCLIP’s backbone was pre-trained on a large, domain-speciﬁc chest radiograph corpus, giving it a narrow advantage in that modality. Comparison with the few-shot methods. Against other few-shot approaches—DRA, BGAD, APRIL-GAN and the recent MVFA, our method achieves the highest class-level AUC on ﬁve of the six benchmarks—HIS, ChestXray, OCT17, LiverCT and RESC. For the pixel-level AUC, TAFT outperforms DRA, BGAD and APRIL-GAN but is slightly inferior to MVFA on LiverCT and RESC dataset. These gains arise from our use of region-level prompts and a dedicated text adapter to inject ﬁne-grained medical semantics, plus a joint contrastive loss that leverages even a handful of abnormal examples to sharpen the normal/abnormal boundary. 4.3 Inﬂuence of Shot Number Fig. 6 Comparisons with state-of-the-art few-shot anomaly-detection methods on six datasets unber diﬀerent shot number. text: In this paper, we propose a novel CLIP-based framework for few-shot medical image anomaly detection, incorporating several eﬀective enhancements to the text encoder and cross-modal fusion process. Speciﬁcally, we introduce region-level prompts to enrich semantic granularity, a lightweight text adapter to improve domain-speciﬁc alignment, and a supervised alignment mechanism to fuse visual and textual features. Additionally, a joint comparison loss is devised to strengthen the discriminative capacity between normal and abnormal cases. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both anomaly classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks, especially under limited supervision. Ablation studies further conﬁrm the contribution of each module. Beyond methodological improvements, recent studies have demonstrated the growing impact of deep learning systems in real-world clinical decision support, such as large-scale imaging-based models for detecting silent brain infarction and predicting stroke risk [40], as well as approaches that integrate image-based deep learning with language models for primary diabetes care [41]. In this study, our work addresses a complementary and foundational problem using the deep learning frameworks, aiming to enable robust medical anomaly detection and localization under limited annotation scenarios. Our work highlights the untapped potential of CLIP’s text encoder and provides new insights into multimodal learning for medical anomaly detection in data-scarce settings.

text: {mahshid.shiri, cigdem.beyan, vittorio.murino}@univr.it Abstract. An innovative few-shot anomaly detection approach is presented, leveraging the pre-trained CLIP model for medical data, and adapting it for both image-level anomaly classification (AC) and pixellevel anomaly segmentation (AS). A dual-branch design is proposed to separately capture normal and abnormal features through learnable adapters in the CLIP vision encoder. To improve semantic alignment, learnable text prompts are employed to link visual features. Furthermore, SigLIP loss is applied to effectively handle the many-to-one relationship between images and unpaired text prompts, showcasing its adaptation in the medical field for the first time. Our approach is validated on multiple modalities, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods for AC and AS, in both same-dataset and cross-dataset evaluations. Unlike prior work, it does not rely on synthetic data or memory banks, and an ablation study confirms the contribution of each component. The code is available at https://github.com/mahshid1998/MadCLIP. Keywords: Medical Anomaly Detection · CLIP · Adapters · Learnable prompts · Few-shot 1
title: MadCLIP: Few-Shot Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP

text: Medical anomaly detection (AD) involves identifying unusual patterns in medical data, a task complicated by the lack of a universal anomaly definition, inconsistent patterns, and noisy data from variably calibrated sensory devices. These challenges are magnified by the crucial role of AD in medical diagnosis, where high sensitivity is essential. Therefore, AD models in medicine must achieve exceptional performance for clinical reliability [8, 28, 34]. Overall, the AD task is approached from two main perspectives in the broader literature: (a) unsupervised techniques (e.g., [6, 26]) and (b) supervised methods (e.g., [13, 35, 32, 31]). Unsupervised methods detect anomalies by leveraging large datasets of normal samples, modeling the normal data distribution, and identifying anomalies as deviations. For example, PatchCore [25] compares test samples to a memory bank of normal embeddings and measures the nearest distance, while CFLOW-AD [9] models normal samples with a Gaussian distribution using normalizing flows. 2 Mahshid Shiri, Cigdem Beyan, and Vittorio Murino While many methods rely on large datasets, real-world applications often include a few labeled anomalies, which provide valuable, application-specific insights and enable recent models to significantly improve the detection of similar anomalies [7]. In this context, supervised methods operate in a few-shot AD setting, where both normal and anomalous samples are limited, e.g., [7, 12, 27, 32]. However, the limited samples available during training, for both normal and anomalous classes, often fail to capture their full variability, restricting the model’s ability to generalize to unseen cases [7]. Recently, CLIP [23] based methods have made significant strides in few-shot AD for medical images, e.g., [35, 13]. It is clear that, relying solely on CLIP [23] is insufficient, as its training focuses on aligning with the class semantics of foreground objects, limiting its ability to generalize and capture subtle visual abnormalities, and restricting its direct application in AD. Also, the substantial distribution shift between the data on which CLIP [23] was trained and medical images results in suboptimal performance when CLIP is applied directly to medical AD [13]. To effectively leverage CLIP for few-shot AD, it is crucial to address the domain gap and fine-tune or adapt CLIP [23] specifically for the medical AD task. For instance, MVFA [13] utilizes visual adapters in the form of fully connected layers, while MediCLIP [35] uses convolutional layers. On the other hand, several studies have shown that leveraging text modality as a representative of normal and abnormal classes can aid AD [16, 5, 35, 13]. Since anomaly descriptions might share similarities across different datasets, incorporating textual information reduces reliance only on visual data and, might enhance model performance, particularly in data-scarce scenarios such as few-shot learning. For instance, WinCLIP [16] uses a large set of artificial text prompts, while April-
title: MadCLIP: Few-Shot Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP

text: as a representative of normal and abnormal classes can aid AD [16, 5, 35, 13]. Since anomaly descriptions might share similarities across different datasets, incorporating textual information reduces reliance only on visual data and, might enhance model performance, particularly in data-scarce scenarios such as few-shot learning. For instance, WinCLIP [16] uses a large set of artificial text prompts, while April- GAN [5] maps visual features extracted from CLIP [23] onto the linear space of text features in addition to using several memory banks. In medical AD, MVFA [13] builds on the principles of April-GAN [5] by employing multi-level adaptation of CLIP and utilizing fixed prompts. Unlike MVFA [13], WinCLIP [16], and April-GAN [5] using fixed prompts, MediCLIP [35] adopts the learnable prompts approach from [36]. Learnable prompts offer a key advantage over fixed prompts, which require careful design and expert knowledge for medical scenarios [35]. Besides visual feature adaptation and text prompts, another common approach is using memory banks (e.g., [5, 13]), though this strategy is relatively costly and often fails to generalize well. Some, e.g., [35], generate extensive synthetic data for the abnormal class to improve generalization. Our approach, MadCLIP extends CLIP [23] with a two-branch architecture using adapters to capture normal and abnormal visual features. We further leverage the role of text in data-scarce scenarios, using it to represent both normal and abnormal distributions separately. MadCLIP is thus designed to learn these distributions from both visual data and text, aiming to obtain a clear distinction between normal and abnormal patterns. As a result, complementary branches exchange signals, and two sets of learnable prompts enable the model to capture distinctive descriptions for both normal and abnormal patterns. text: Few-shot medical AD is based on a dataset consisting of tuples {(x, c, M)}, where each x ∈Rh×w×3 represents a training image with spatial dimensions h × w, c ∈{0, 1} denotes the image-level AC label (1 for anomalous, 0 for normal), and, when available, M ∈{0, 1}h×w provides the pixel-level AS map. The training set is balanced, ensuring that |{x | c = 0}| = |{x | c = 1}|. Given a test image xtest, the model predicts both AC and AS. Building on this setup, we propose MadCLIP (see Fig. 1), a novel approach that leverages CLIP [23], incorporating multi-level visual features adaptation and learnable text prompts to enhance performance. MadCLIP is a dual-branch architecture that learns separate multi-modal representations for normal and abnormal samples. Below, we provide a detailed description of the components employed in MadCLIP. Vision Adapters. MadCLIP employs adapters (denoted as Ai n and Ai ab for normal and abnormal samples, respectively) within the CLIP vision encoder, which is pre-trained on natural images [23], to effectively adapt it for medical imaging and the two target tasks: AC and AS. Using adapters follows the findings of [13], which shows that it is preferable to traditional fine-tuning, as it helps avoid overfitting due to high model complexity and limited data. Our adapters are integrated while keeping the backbone frozen. In detail, for an input image x, we extract the i-th layer feature from the CLIP vision encoder, denoted as Ii(x) ∈RG×d. Here, G represents the grid size, d is the feature dimension, and i ∈{6, 12, 18, 24}. Learnable adapters consist of two transformation stages. The first stage focuses on addressing the domain gap between natural and medical images. Since CLIP embeddings are inherently optimized for object-level tasks in natural images, they may not directly align with the requirements of medical AD. To bridge this gap, we introduce a shared linear transformation layer (W i shared) that refines the CLIP embeddings, mapping them into a feature space better suited for medical AD, formulated as F i shared(Ii(x)) = ReLU(W i sharedIi(x)). The second stage, given the need to perform both AC and AS, focuses on extracting features specialized for each task, we apply two distinct linear transformation heads on top of the shared features: the first head, dedicated to AC, captures high-level characteristics essential for detecting anomalies, while the second head, tailored for AS, emphasizes finegrained spatial details, expressed as F i Det(Ii(x)) = ReLU  W i det F i shared(Ii(x))  and F i Seg(Ii(x)) = ReLU  W i Seg F i shared(Ii(x))  . Learnable Prompts. Prior works have shown that well-designed text prompts in CLIP can encapsulate rich semantic information, resulting in

text: while the second head, tailored for AS, emphasizes finegrained spatial details, expressed as F i Det(Ii(x)) = ReLU  W i det F i shared(Ii(x))  and F i Seg(Ii(x)) = ReLU  W i Seg F i shared(Ii(x))  . Learnable Prompts. Prior works have shown that well-designed text prompts in CLIP can encapsulate rich semantic information, resulting in more reliable and transferable representations for several tasks [20]. By using learnable prompts, e.g., [36], we can eliminate the complexity of manually engineered prompts, which we argue that it leads to better generalization of the resulting text embeddings to medical imaging tasks. Additionally, we posit that these prompts can provide complementary signals between our dual branches, enhancing AD MadCLIP: Few-shot Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP 5 performance. Standard prompts such as “A photo of a [CLS]” primarily capture the overall semantic content of images, which often fails to reflect the subtle, domain-specific details found in medical imaging [37, 13]. To address this limitation, we develop a template for the normal (pn) and abnormal (pab) classes as: pn = [V1][V2] . . . [VM][CLS(normal)][Objective], pab = [W1][W2] . . . [WM] [CLS(abnormal)][Objective] where [Vi] and [Wi] denote learnable token embeddings, [CLS(normal)] and [CLS(abnormal)] are fixed class embeddings, and [Objective] encodes the fixed semantic context of the target modality (e.g., Brain). To further enhance AD, we leverage an ensemble of text prompts by incorporating multiple synonyms for normal (e.g. flawless, unblemished) and abnormal (e.g. with a flaw, disease). Each synonym generates a distinct prompt, leading to two prompt sets, Pn = {pn1, pn2, . . . , pnk} and Pab = {pab1, pab2, . . . , pabk}, where k represents the number of synonyms. By aggregating the diverse textual prompts from these sets, we obtain two final prompts, tn and tab. Dual Branch Architecture. In few-shot AD, normal samples xn are assumed to be drawn from an unknown distribution Dn (i.e., xn ∼Dn), while anomalous samples xab originate from a distinct, typically unknown distribution Dab. These two distributions are roughly complementary such that Dab = 1 −Dn, based on the assumption that anomalies are defined as deviations from normal data. Our dual-branch architecture processes these distributions via two specialized branches.The so-called normality branch extracts features from normal samples and aligns them with a learnable text prompt tn, capturing the behavior of Dn. In parallel, the so-called abnormality branch processes abnormal samples and aligns the extracted features with a complementary prompt tab. Each branch is trained to maximize the cosine similarity (cosSIM) between its visual features and the corresponding prompt while minimizing similarity with the opposing prompt (i.e., representative of the opposite class). Formally, for a normal sample xn, adapters Ai n

text: Dn. In parallel, the so-called abnormality branch processes abnormal samples and aligns the extracted features with a complementary prompt tab. Each branch is trained to maximize the cosine similarity (cosSIM) between its visual features and the corresponding prompt while minimizing similarity with the opposing prompt (i.e., representative of the opposite class). Formally, for a normal sample xn, adapters Ai n produce feature representations Oi n = Ai n �Ii(xn)  . The dual optimization objective for normal samples is to maximize cosSIM(Oi n, tn) −cosSIM(Oi n, tab), which, assuming cosine similarity approximates the dot product, simplifies to max  Oi n · tn −Oi n · tab  . An analogous formulation is used for abnormal samples: max  Oi ab · tab −Oi ab · tn  . These objectives aim to enforce a clear separation between the normal and abnormal feature spaces. Furthermore, at each feature layer i, the normality and abnormality scores are computed as Si n =  Oi n · tn −Oi n · tab  and Si ab =  Oi ab · tab −Oi ab · tn  and then concatenated into a single vector Si =  Si n, Si ab  . The composite loss function we use at feature level i is Li = λ1 Dice( ˆ M i, M) + λ2 Focal( ˆ M i, M) + λ3 SigLip(ˆci, c) where ˆ M i represents the predicted anomaly map and ˆci is the predicted anomaly score at the i’th feature level, M is the ground truth mask, and c denotes the image-level anomaly label. The hyperparameters λ1, λ2, and λ3 are fixed to 1. Dice(., .), Focal(., .), and SigLip(., .) correspond to Dice [22], Focal [24], and a sigmoid-based loss for text-image alignment [33]. text: the image-level anomaly label. The hyperparameters λ1, λ2, and λ3 are fixed to 1. Dice(., .), Focal(., .), and SigLip(., .) correspond to Dice [22], Focal [24], and a sigmoid-based loss for text-image alignment [33]. The Dice and Focal losses are necessary for AS, and particularly Focal loss is preferred as there is a significant class imbalance at the pixel level, with anomalous pixels being greatly outnumbered by normal pixels. Instead, for the AC task, given the balanced classes, the adaptation of SigLip [33] is sufficient. The overall loss L is computed as the sum of losses across all feature levels: L = P i Li. We use SigLip loss [33] instead of the original CLIP loss[23] because our architecture introduces two learnable text embeddings, each linked to multiple images. Specifically, image similarity is computed across both normal and abnormal prompts, while each prompt is compared against all images. This results in a similarity matrix capturing multiple valid associations rather than a strict diagonal mapping. While CLIP loss can compute image similarity across all texts, it cannot directly handle text similarity across multiple images, as each text embedding corresponds to multiple images in a batch. In contrast, SigLip loss processes image-text pairs independently, naturally supporting our many-to-one setup. This distinguishes our approach from previous work in medical AD [31, 11, 35, 13], with its contribution experimentally validated below. 3 Experimental Analysis and Results We follow the latest SOTA: MVFA [13], using a medical AD benchmark that spans five modalities and six datasets: brain MRI [1, 2, 21], liver CT [4, 19], retinal OCT (composed of two datasets; OCT17 [17], and RESC [10]), chest Xray (Chest) [30], and digital histopathology (HIS) [3]. BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC are used for both AC and AS, while OCT17, Chest, and HIS are relevant only for AC. We use the area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC), the standard medical AD metric, to report AUC for AC and AUC for AS. Implementation Details. We use the CLIP model with the ViT-L/14 architecture and 240-pixel input images, as in [13]. The model has 24 layers and the adapters were applied to the 6th, 12th, 18th, and 24th layers. Training is performed with the Adam optimizer with the learning rate of 1e−3, batch size 16, for 60 epochs. Augmentation follows the strategy outlined in [13]. Comparisons with SOTA. text: We introduced a few-shot AD architecture that leverages CLIP with multi-level adapters and prompt learning to model normal and abnormal classes separately. Our dual-objective strategy, formulated through subtraction, incorporates a contrastive effect by encouraging similarity within the same class and dissimilarity MadCLIP: Few-shot Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP 9 between opposing class. By integrating SigLIP loss, we further refine this separation process, as it can handle many-to-one relationship of images and learnable unpaired texts. Extensive validation across diverse datasets demonstrates superior performance and strong generalization over SOTA methods, underscoring our approach’s robustness for medical AD. However, a current limitation of MadCLIP is the assumption that learnable adapters and prompts are sufficient to bridge the gap between medical images and textual descriptions, while the modality gap remains unaddressed explicitly. Future work will explore the method’s zero-shot potential and extend it to multi-modal AD, handling diverse training modalities and unseen anatomical regions simultaneously. Acknowledgments. text: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) identifies anomalies without needing training samples from the target dataset, essential for scenarios with privacy concerns or limited data. Vision-language models like CLIP show potential in ZSAD but have limitations: relying on manually crafted fixed textual descriptions or anomaly prompts is time-consuming and prone to semantic ambiguity, and CLIP struggles with pixel-level anomaly segmentation, focusing more on global semantics than local details. To address these limitations, We introduce KAnoCLIP, a novel ZSAD framework that leverages vision-language models. KAnoCLIP combines general knowledge from a Large Language Model (GPT-3.5) and fine-grained, image-specific knowledge from a Visual Question Answering system (Llama3) via Knowledge-Driven Prompt Learning (KnPL). KnPL uses a knowledge-driven (KD) loss function to create learnable anomaly prompts, removing the need for fixed text prompts and enhancing generalization. KAnoCLIP includes the CLIP visual encoder with V-V attention (CLIP-VV), Bi-Directional Cross- Attention for Multi-Level Cross-Modal Interaction (Bi-CMCI), and Conv-Adapter. These components preserve local visual semantics, improve local cross-modal fusion, and align global visual features with textual information, enhancing pixel-level anomaly detection. text: Anomaly detection (AD) [1, 2] is crucial in fields like industrial quality assurance, medical diagnostics, and video analysis, encompassing anomaly classification (AC) and anomaly segmentation (AS) for image-level and pixel-level anomalies. The main challenges in AD are the rarity and diversity of anomalies, making dataset collection costly and time-consuming. Traditional one-class or unsupervised methods [2] often fall short due to the diverse and long-tail distribution of anomalies across domains such as industrial defects and medical lesions, necessitating a generalizable model. Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) [3–5] is vital for identifying anomalies without extensive training samples, particularly when data privacy concerns or insufficient labeled data are issues. Vision-Language Models (VLMs), like CLIP [6], have advanced ZSAD by leveraging training on large datasets of image-text pairs. † Corresponding author However, CLIP’s original model still faces challenges in anomaly detection due to the task’s complexity. There are two main limitations in applying CLIP to zero-shot anomaly detection: (1) existing

text: [3, 4, 6, 7] rely on fixed text descriptions or anomaly prompts. For zero-shot anomaly detection using CLIP, a commonly used text prompt template is "a photo of a [class] with holes." However, these handcrafted prompts require extensive expertise, are time-consuming, and suffer from semantic ambiguity. Inspired by prompt learning in NLP, CoOp [8] utilizes learnable vectors for prompts and requires only a few labeled images. Despite this, CoOp tends to overfit to base classes, thus diminishing its ability to generalize to unseen classes. (2) while CLIP aligns image-level semantics with anomaly prompts through cross-modal contrastive training, it performs poorly in precise anomaly segmentation (pixel-level detection) because it emphasizes global semantics and overlooks local details [3, 6]. A mechanism for refining CLIP models in the local visual space and integrating local pixel-level cross-modal features is necessary for superior anomaly segmentation. To address the two main limitations, we propose the KAnoCLIP framework, which introduces KnPL. This approach leverages large language model (LLM) and a visual question answering (VQA) system to generate anomaly descriptions, forming a knowledge base that guides the development of Learnable Normal Prompts (LNPs) and Learnable Abnormal Prompts (LAPs) using KD loss. This Loss minimizes the Euclidean distance between LLM-VQA-generated abnormal prompts and LAPs while maximizing the distance to LNPs, effectively eliminating the reliance on fixed text prompts and enhancing generalization to new anomaly classes. Furthermore, the framework integrates CLIP-VV, Bi-CMCI, and Conv-Adapter to preserve local visual semantics, improve cross-modal fusion, and align global visual features with textual information. These enhancements collectively improve the detection of subtle anomalies. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • KAnoCLIP is a novel zero-shot anomaly detection solution that doesn’t require training samples from the target dataset, making it ideal for applications with privacy concerns or limited data, especially in industrial and medical fields. • We introduce knowledge-driven prompt learning to eliminate manual text prompting and alleviate overfitting, thereby enhancing generalization to new anomaly classes. • KAnoCLIP integrates CLIP-VV, Bi-CMCI, and Con-Adapter to refine local visual spaces and enhance cross-modal interactions, achieving robust pixel-level anomaly segmentation. • Extensive experiments on 12 industrial and medical datasets demonstrate that KAnoCLIP consistently outperforms stateof-the-art techniques, setting a new benchmark for ZSAD. arXiv:2501.03786v1 [cs.CV] 7 Jan 2025 Nomal Text Features (Fn) Abnormal Text Features (Fa) CLIP Text Encoder (GLobal Anomaly Score) Max Anomaly Map Global Visual Feature Stage1 Stage3 Stage2 Learnable Frozen Element-wise sum Matrix Multiplication CLIP（Original）Image encoder V-V attention CLIP visual encoder with V-V attention (CLIP-VV) Stage4 Conv-Adapter V-V Attention V-V Attention V-V Attention V-V Attention Local Visual Feature Learnable Normal Prompts (LNPs) Learnable Abnormal Prompts (LAPs) [A1][A2]···[Ak][Abnormal][CLASS] [N1][N2]···[Nk][Normal][CLASS] Knowledge-Driven Prompt Learning (KnPL) CLIP Text Encoder Ground truth Fine-grained image-specific knowledge generated by VQA General knowledge

text: As shown in Figure 1, our KAnoCLIP framework introduces Knowledge-Driven Prompt Learning to remove the need for fixed text prompts and enhance generalization. By integrating CLIP-VV, Bi-CMCI, and Conv-Adapter, KAnoCLIP enhances local visual features, cross-modal interactions. These innovations significantly improve zero-shot anomaly detection performance. During training, the KAnoCLIP framework minimizes the loss function Ltotal in Equation 13 using an auxiliary anomaly detection dataset. During inference, a test image xi is processed through the CLIP-VV visual encoder to extract patch features F i patch. LNPs and LAPs, previously learned normal and abnormal text prompts, are inputted into the CLIP text encoder to extract text features Ftext. These patch and text features are combined in the Bi-CMCI module to generate an anomaly map Mi ∈RH×W for each layer. The maps are summed and normalized to create the final anomaly map M. After adjusting global visual features using the Conv-Adapter, the maximum value of M determines the global anomaly score.

KgCoOp [9] found that performance drops are linked to the distance between learnable (CoOp) and fixed (CLIP) prompts. By reducing this distance, generalization improves. Inspired by KgCoOp, we initially used fixed CLIP prompts (e.g., "a photo of an abnormal [class]") to guide learnable anomaly prompts, but this failed due to insufficient anomaly knowledge. We propose combining LLMs’ general knowledge with VLMs’ detailed image descriptions to create a knowledge-driven prompt learning (KnPL) method for zero-shot anomaly detection. section: 2.3 Refining Local Visual Space with V-V Attention
text: The original CLIP visual encoder, pre-trained with contrastive loss, produces global embeddings and uses a Q-K self-attention mechanism that disrupts local visual semantics, impairing fine-grained anomaly detection. To address this, we introduce a V-V attention mechanism [10] into the CLIP visual encoder, enhancing the extraction of local visual features crucial for pixel-level anomaly segmentation without altering the original structure. V-V attention preserves local visual semantics by focusing on relationships between local features, resulting in attention maps with a distinct diagonal pattern. text: We propose the Bi-Directional Cross-Attention for Multi-Level Cross-Modal Interaction (Bi-CMCI) and Conv-Adapter to address the limitations of traditional cross-modal feature fusion methods, such as linear layer projections [7]. These traditional methods often struggle to capture complex interactions and dependencies between visual and textual modalities, which are crucial for effective anomaly detection. Bi-CMCI manages local cross-modal interactions, while Conv-Adapter aligns global features. This dual approach effectively captures both local details and global context, thereby enhancing the model’s accuracy in detecting subtle anomalies. Bi-CMCI. As illustrated in Figure 1 and 3, Bi-CMCI employs a bi-directional cross-attention (BiCA) [11] mechanism to align textual descriptions with visual parts through Text-to-Visual Cross- Attention and refine text with local visual features via Visual-to-Text Cross-Attention. Self-Attention ensures independent understanding within each modality, while Deformable Self-Attention [12] adapts to key visual parts, addressing variations in shape and position. Bi-CMCI operates across the four stages of the CLIP-VV visual encoder to capture multi-level detailed information for identifying subtle anomalies. Each stage extracts intermediate patch-level features F i patch ∈RHiWi×Ci. The LNPs and LAPs are input into the CLIP Text Encoder g(·), producing text features representing normal and abnormal cases, Ftext = [Fn, Fa] ∈R2×C. The Bi- CMCI module then deeply fuses the cross-modal features F i patch and Ftext, resulting in the normal map M n i ∈RH×W , anomaly map M a i ∈RH×W , and the final localization result M. Norm(·) normalizes the anomaly map values to the range of 0 to 1. Gσ is a Gaussian filter with σ controlling the smoothing. Conv-Adapter. As illustrated in Figure 4, the Conv-Adapter uses a depthwise separable convolution bottleneck [13] to better align global visual and textual features. It includes three main components: depthwise convolution for capturing spatial features, activation functions for nonlinearity, and pointwise convolution for dimensionality reduction and efficiency. text: We develop joint optimization, a method for effectively learning knowledge-driven text prompts from both global and local perspectives. The total loss function Ltotal is defined as follows: Ltotal = αLKD + βLglobal + γLlocal, (13) where the hyperparameters α, β, and γ balance the three loss components, and we default all of them to 1. Global Loss (Lglobal). The global loss is a binary cross-entropy loss that matches the cosine similarity between text embeddings and visual embeddings from auxiliary data of normal/anomalous images. Lglobal = BCE(Sglobal, Label), (14) where Sglobal represents the global anomaly score as calculated in equation 12, and Label indicates whether the image is anomalous. Local Loss (Llocal). The local loss combines focal loss [14] and dice loss [15] to handle fine-grained local anomalous regions in the intermediate layers of the visual encoder. Llocal = Focal(M a, G) + Dice(M n, I −G) + Dice(M a, G), (15) where G ∈RH×W is the ground truth segmentation mask, with Gij = 1 for anomalous pixels and Gij = 0 otherwise. I denotes a matrix of ones. text: Datasets. We conducted experiments on 12 datasets, covering industrial and medical anomaly detection. Industrial datasets included MVTec-AD [16] , VisA [17], MPDD [18], BTAD [19], SDD [20], and DAGM [21]. Medical datasets were BrainMRI [22], LiverCT [23], RESC [24], Br35H [25], COVID-19 [26], and HeadCT [22]. Evaluation Metrics. We used the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) for evaluation, applying image-level AUC for classification and pixel-level AUC for segmentation. Baselines. Our KAnoCLIP was thoroughly compared with state-ofthe-art methods, including CLIP [6], CLIP-AC [6], WinCLIP [4], APRIL-GAN [7], MVFA-AD [3], and AnomalyCLIP [5]. Implementation details. We used the CLIP model (VIT-L/14@336px) as our backbone, keeping all parameters frozen. Following APRIL- GAN and AnomalyCLIP, we trained our model on the MVTec-AD test data and evaluated the ZSAD performance on other datasets. Learnable word embeddings length was set to 12. Experiments were conducted in PyTorch 2.0.0 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.

text: In this paper, we introduce KAnoCLIP, a zero-shot anomaly detection framework using KnPL, which integrates LLM’s general knowledge with VQA system’s image-specific insights to create learnable anomaly prompts, eliminating fixed text prompts and enhancing generalization to new anomaly classes. KAnoCLIP employs three modules: CLIP-VV, Bi-CMCI, and Conv-Adapter, optimizing visual space, cross-modal interactions, and global-local context integration. Extensive experiments on 12 industrial and medical datasets show that KAnoCLIP consistently outperforms SOTA methods, demonstrating superior generalization capabilities.

The CLIP model, renowned for its exceptional transferability and multimodal comprehension prowess honed through pre-training on vast image-text datasets, faces hurdles in the medical domain due to the confidentiality, intricacy, and scarcity of medical imagery and associated reports. To surmount these obstacles, this study introduces the CLIPDxNet framework, ingeniously merging classical Convolutional Neural Networks and sophisticated attention mechanisms with the CLIP model to amplify its capacity for discerning intricate details in medical images and concentrating on vital regions of interest. CLIPDxNet embraces a decoupled image-text contrastive learning schema for medical data, complemented by meticulous data augmentation techniques and refined training methodologies, thereby optimizing the utilization of scarce medical datasets and fortifying the model's generalization aptitudes and zero-shot inference capabilities. The experimental results indicate the outstanding performance of CLIPDxNet in anomaly detection and lesion localization across diverse medical image datasets, surpassing extant methodologies. Moreover, the paper delves into the expansive applicability of the CLIP model in areas such as medical image segmentation, outlining prospective avenues for upcoming research endeavors.

text: In the pursuit of advancing visual language encoders, a pivotal aspect lies in efficiently extracting semantically aligned information from both visual and linguistic data. CLIP[1], standing out as an exemplary visual language encoder, has garnered significant attention for its remarkable versatility. Not only has CLIP[1] demonstrated unprecedented high-quality performance in text-to-image generation tasks, but it has also significantly propelled the progression of multimodal understanding tasks, showcasing substantial impacts within the realms of computer vision and natural language processing. This pre-training model, which trains on large-scale image-text pairs, generates transferable representations capable of supporting a diverse array of downstream tasks. Numerous studies have illuminated[2] that this joint learning fosters favorable influences across various visual tasks downstream, including knowledge classification[3], open-world segmentation[4], textto-image synthesis[5], video text detection[6][7], among others. However, given the IIPA-2025 Journal of Physics: Conference Series 3212 (2026) 012009 IOP Publishing doi:10.1088/1742-6596/3212/1/012009 2 privacy and intricacy inherent to medical images and reports, these images – such as X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans – diverge notably from conventional image data. They possess not only a high degree of specialization but also encompass a wealth of detailed information vital for diagnosis and treatment. Medical reports, too, are highly specialized, embedding a plethora of medical jargon and meticulous descriptions. This combination of privacy and intricacy poses unique challenges for implementing CLIP models in the medical domain, while simultaneously presenting novel opportunities. The knowledge co-learned from medical images and reports facilitates downstream clinical tasks, and Zifeng Wang et al.[8] observed that while the CLIP model[1] employs contrastive learning in its training, this approach does not adequately attend to the nuances in imaging details. Trained on a colossal dataset comprising 4 billion image-text pairs sourced entirely from the internet, the model confronts a stark contrast with the scarce availability of publicly accessible medical images and reports. Moreover, medical images and reports bear unique characteristics; the distinctions within the medical realm are subtler and finer-grained compared to general image-text pairs. Thus, when applying visual-text pre-training techniques in medicine, addressing the paucity of data and capturing the subtle yet crucial medical nuances is imperative. To this end, researchers introduced MedCLIP[8], a model tailored to effectively tackle the challenges posed by the scarcity and fine-grained specificity of medical image and text data. MedCLIP enhances representation capabilities and generalization performance, enabling zero-shot prediction, and demonstrates competence in supervised classification and image-text retrieval tasks. By decoupling images from text, MedCLIP facilitates contrastive learning on a large volume of non-paired data while incorporating medical knowledge for semantic alignment, thereby mitigating misclassification issues. However, MedCLIP[8] encounters

text: in accurately identifying and localizing pathological regions. In response, MediCLIP[9] was developed, which trains on synthesized abnormal images instead of relying on real abnormal images. These synthetic images, crafted through meticulously designed abnormality synthesis tasks, effectively emulate the myriad of anomaly patterns encountered in medical imaging. Despite the advancements and refinements brought about by MediCLIP[9], there remains room for enhancing its generality and scalability. This paper delves into exploring innovative ways of effectively integrating traditional mechanisms such as convolution and attention with the CLIP model, thereby furthering our understanding of the diverse anomaly patterns observed in medical imaging and enhancing the capacity for multi-scale lesion localization. The CLIPDxNet framework emerges as a direct response to this pursuit during the endeavor to fuse conventional convolutional, attention-based mechanisms with the CLIP model. Within this framework, we propose methodologies that address compatibility issues between these components, ensuring their seamless collaboration and collective contribution to improved model performance. By incorporating the local feature extraction prowess of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and the focus on salient regions enabled by attention mechanisms, we aspire to augment the CLIP model's comprehension and representation of medical images. This integration aims to refine the model's ability to discern intricate details and contextually relevant features within medical imagery, thereby pushing the boundaries of diagnostic precision and the interpretability of medical imaging results. section: 1.1 Innovative Fusion of Conventional Techniques with CLIP
text: We propose the CLIPDxNet model, ingeniously integrating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) renowned for their prowess in local feature extraction, along with advanced attention mechanisms such as ODConv, to reinforce the model's precise capture and representation of details in medical images. This fusion strategy not only exploits the CNN's strength in image detail analysis but also leverages attention mechanisms to focus the model more acutely on critical pathological regions in medical images, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy and reliability of disease identification. Our aim through this innovative fusion is to combine the strengths of traditional computer vision techniques with the powerful visual-linguistic understanding capabilities of the CLIP model, providing a more accurate, efficient, and dependable solution for medical image analysis.

Concurrently, we implemented refined training strategies, including the selection of optimal loss functions and tuning of optimizer parameters, with the objective of maximizing the utilization of finite medical image data. This significantly enhances the model's generalization capacity, ensuring robust performance and excellence in practical applications.

text: In recent years, technologies exemplified by the GPT series [10][11][12] have made significant strides in Natural Language Processing (NLP), leading to the evolution and eventual emergence of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Concurrently, researchers have embarked on exploring whether the visual domain can spawn largescale models akin to those in NLP, with the ambition of comprehending diverse scenarios in the open world. The core objective of "open-world scenes" revolves around recognizing any concept in the open world, a notion referred to as "open vocabulary," implying that the target vocabulary is not statically enclosed but continually expanding. During its training phase, CLIP learns the alignment between images and text, and subsequently, during inference, it leverages this alignment to match images with their corresponding textual categories, thereby enabling zero- shot classification. The emergence of CLIP has opened up possibilities for tasks such as object detection [13], image captioning [14], and semantic segmentation [15] within the realm of open-world visual settings, facilitating advanced understanding and processing of visual data in diverse real- world contexts. Visual-text representation learning has been shown to be capable of learning effective visual representations, performing well in general domains. However, it heavily relies on large-scale web image and caption datasets, and does not inherently support crossmodal retrieval or zero-shot prediction. In recent years, there have been significant advancements in medical image anomaly detection [16][17], with some tasks achieving anomaly detection performance comparable to or even surpassing that of professional clinical doctors. Nevertheless, the limited scale of medical image-text data hampers the implementation of self-supervised learning in this field. Although remedies exist, the required data volume still vastly exceeds what is typically available in medical datasets. ZHANG Y et al. [18] investigated medical image-text representation learning but were constrained by computational power and data availability, failing to resolve issues with false-negative noise. The MedCLIP model [8] utilizes medical knowledge tailored to mitigate false negatives in contrastive learning, thereby improving the efficiency of pre-training data. This decoupled framework for contrastive learning between medical images and texts effectively addresses the scarcity and subtlety of differences in medical image and text datasets, enhancing the model's representational capabilities and generalizability. This model incorporates text prompts of unrelated objects to learn common normal and abnormal features in images, unaffected by object semantics. Mutual-Channel Loss (MC-Loss) [23] is a loss function based on channel interaction, designed for fine-grained image classification tasks. It comprises two channel-specific components: a discriminative component and a diversity component. The discriminative component enforces all feature channels within the same class to be discriminative through a novel channel attention mechanism. Conversely, the diversity component constraints channels to be mutually repulsive in the spatial dimension. MC-Loss allows for end-to-end training without requiring any bounding box/part annotations and yields highly discriminative regions during inference. In the realm of anomaly detection in medical imaging, MC- Loss also demonstrates its unique potential. Medical images, such as X-rays, CT scans, and MRI images, frequently encompass intricate structures and subtle abnormal features, posing stringent demands on the precision of anomaly detection. Its strength lies in the end-to-end training methodology, which does not rely on any bounding boxes or part annotations, enabling the Figure 2. MC-Loss illustration. text: Omni-dimensional Dynamic Convolution (ODConv) [22] represents an innovative multidimensional attention mechanism coupled with a parallel strategy, which is incorporated into our proposed CLIPDxNet framework. This strategy comprehensively takes into account four pivotal dimensions: the number of convolution kernels, spatial size, input channels, and output channels, enabling the learning of complementary attention mechanisms and realizing dynamic convolutions across all these dimensions. This design significantly bolsters the model's adaptability and accuracy, particularly when confronted with intricate medical image data. Departing from conventional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that utilize fixed convolution kernels for operations, ODConv [22] renders every convolution kernel a trainable parameter. Consequently, the model can dynamically adjust convolution kernels based on varying image content and locations, thereby capturing local Figure 3. This capability of dynamic adjustment markedly enhances the precision of image recognition and medical anomaly detection. Furthermore, ODConv [22] is capable of handling multi-channel inputs, allowing each channel to have its own set of convolution kernels. Such a design not only enriches feature diversity but also augments the model's generalization capacity when dealing with diverse medical images. Whether confronted with common pathologies or rare abnormalities, ODConv furnishes more robust and accurate detection outcomes. Fig. 3 illustrates the schematic diagram of the ODConv structure. It can be described as follow: y = (αs1⨀αc1⨀αf1⨀αω1⨀W1 + . . . + αsn⨀αcn⨀αfn⨀αωn⨀Wn) ∗x. (7) Among them, αsi , αci , and αfi represent attentions along the spatial dimension, input channel dimension, and output channel dimension, respectively, while αωi denotes the attention scalar for convolution kernel Wi . These four types of attentions complement one another and cumulatively apply to convolution kernel Wi in sequence based on position, channel, filter, and order of convolution kernels, rendering the convolution operation unique for every spatial location, input channel, filter, and convolution kernel across input x. Consequently, ODConv dramatically enhances the feature extraction capability of conventional CNN convolution operations, capturing richer contextual information. Serving as a direct substitute for traditional convolutions, ODConv can be seamlessly integrated into most Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures. In our case, we introduce ODConv prior to the image encoding stage in the CLIP [1] model. This feature positions ODConv as a potent tool for boosting the performance of existing medical image analysis systems, promising more precise and reliable. When addressing source tasks, to compute the radius of abnormal regions in arbitrary orientations, elliptical or rectangular masks of random sizes and rotation angles are employed. text: CLIPDxNet represents an innovative application of CLIP to medical image anomaly detection by combining CNNs with attention mechanisms (ODConv) and multi-scale lesion localization strategies. This approach significantly enhances medical image analysis capabilities, offering more precise and efficient solutions for disease identification. However, this work represents only initial exploration of CLIP's potential in medical imaging. CLIP applications extend far beyond anomaly detection, particularly in segmentation tasks. Recent advances include open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation using text-image diffusion models [24], CLIP fine-tuning methods for masked image classification [25], GroupViT's zero-shot semantic segmentation capabilities [26], and MaskCLIP's integration of mask tokens with pre-trained ViT CLIP models [27]. CLIP demonstrates immense potential in open-world semantic and instance segmentation. Given medical imaging data scale challenges, significant opportunities exist for CLIP applications in zero-shot/few-shot medical scenarios, representing a crucial direction for future research.

text: Visual Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to identify abnormal samples in images that deviate from normal patterns, covering multiple domains, including industrial, logical, and medical fields. Due to the domain gaps between these fields, existing VAD methods are typically tailored to each domain, with specialized detection techniques and model architectures that are difficult to generalize across different domains. Moreover, even within the same domain, current VAD approaches often follow a “one-category-one-model” paradigm, requiring large amounts of normal samples to train class-specific models, resulting in poor generalizability and hindering unified evaluation across domains. To address this issue, we propose a generalized few-shot VAD method, UniVAD, capable of detecting anomalies across various domains, such as industrial, logical, and medical anomalies, with a training-free unified model. Uni- VAD only needs few normal samples as references during testing to detect anomalies in previously unseen objects, without training on the specific domain. Specifically, UniVAD employs a Contextual Component Clustering (C3) module based on clustering and vision foundation models to segment components within the image accurately, and leverages Component-Aware Patch Matching (CAPM) and Graph-Enhanced Component Modeling (GECM) modules to detect anomalies at different semantic levels, which are aggregated to produce the final detection result. We conduct experiments on nine datasets spanning industrial, logical, and medical fields, and the results demonstrate that UniVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot anomaly detection tasks across multiple domains, outperforming domain-specific anomaly detection models. text: Visual Anomaly Detection (VAD) [11, 19, 29, 36] is a critical task that seeks to identify abnormal samples in images that deviate from established normal patterns, leveraging computer vision techniques [13, 27]. Such anomalies are rare occurrences but signify critical conditions, including errors, defects, or lesions, that necessitate timely intervention for further analysis. VAD spans multiple fields and 1 arXiv:2412.03342v3 [cs.CV] 10 Mar 2025 has applications across diverse industries, such as industrial anomaly detection [11, 19, 29], logical anomaly detection [14, 21, 25], and medical anomaly detection [2, 16]. However, significant variations in data distributions and anomaly types across domains result in current VAD methods [2, 25, 29] being highly specialized for specific domains, often employing custom detection algorithms and model architectures. Consequently, methods optimized for one domain tend to perform poorly in others. For instance, one of the state-of-the-art industrial anomaly detection methods, PatchCore [29], achieves a 1-shot imagelevel AUC of 84.1% on the industrial dataset MVTec- AD [4]. However, its performance drops significantly to 62.0% when applied to the MVTec LOCO [5] dataset for logical anomaly detection. Furthermore, even within the same domain, most contemporary VAD approaches adopt a “one-category-one-model” paradigm, where a separate model is trained for each object category. Once trained, each model is limited to the specific object category. This domain- and category-specific approach constrains VAD research’s standardization and scalability. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free generalized anomaly detection method, UniVAD, which leverages a unified model to detect anomalies across multiple domains. UniVAD can handle industrial, logical, medical, and other anomalies without requiring domain-specific data training. Instead, UniVAD requires only a few normal samples of the target category during the testing phase to perform anomaly detection. This approach significantly enhances the generalizability and transferability of anomaly detection models, as illustrated in Figure 1. Specifically, UniVAD utilizes a contextual component clustering module, incorporating clustering techniques [25] and visual foundation models [17, 22, 24] to segment components within an image. Following this, UniVAD applies a component-aware patch-matching module and a graphenhanced component modeling module to detect anomalies at various semantic levels. The component-aware patchmatching module identifies anomalies such as structural defects or tissue lesions by matching patch-level features within each component. Meanwhile, the graph-enhanced component modeling module employs graph-based component feature aggregation to model relationships between image components, facilitating the detection of more complex logical anomalies, such as missing, added, or incorrect components, through inter-component feature matching. Our experiments, conducted across nine datasets covering industrial, logical, and medical domains, such as MVTec-AD [4], VisA [38], MVTec LOCO [5], Brain MRI [1], and Liver CT [6, 23], demonstrate that UniVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot anomaly detection across multiple domains, significantly outperforming domain-specific models. Our contributions are listed as follows: • We introduce the first training-free unified few-shot visual anomaly detection method capable of detecting anomalies across industrial, logical, and medical domains. This unified approach reduces the significant workload to develop separate detection methods and model architectures for each domain, thereby promoting the standardization of anomaly detection research. • We design a contextual component clustering module that effectively segments object components under fewshot learning conditions. Additionally, combined with our component-aware patch matching module and graphenhanced component modeling module, UniVAD reliably detects anomalies across different semantic levels. • Comprehensive experiments on nine datasets spanning industrial, logical, and medical domains demonstrate that UniVAD achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot anomaly detection, establishing its effectiveness and generalizability across domains.
